field: transformsOf, tense transform, rendered answer for bank:u59-1046 (also u59-1064, u59-1020, u59-1057, u59-1074, u60-t-word-order-style rows)
quote: Ayer cuidá a tu hermano mientras yo salí.
problem: The tense transform prepends Ayer or Antes to whatever parses as a present-tense clause and marks the result as the one right answer. An imperative stays imperative (Ayer cuidá...), a second verb stays in the present (Antes Vos no tenés idea de lo bonito que era Medellín de noche), a fragment becomes nonsense (Ayer Tinto, que hizo frío), and a frequency phrase collides with a single day (Ayer Raras veces llamó Tomás a su mamá). Of the 15 tense transforms seen in 16 rendered days at u59 and u60, 10 are ungrammatical or nonsense and none is natural. The learner must type these to pass.
authority: grammatical reasoning: an imperative has no past; Ayer cannot scope over raras veces

field: transformsOf, negate transform, rendered answer for bank:u60-t-word-order-style-0039 (also ¿Raras veces no cocinas tú en casa? from -0025, Contá cómo no te fue con el abogado from u59-1048)
quote: Poco no me sirvió, la verdad.
problem: The generator produces exactly the error that g:word-order-style lists as a pitfall (Poco no importa ya: "a double negative that Spanish does not use here") and accepts it as correct. The negate transform inserts no before the first finite verb without knowing that poco and raras veces already carry negative force, or that the negation in Contá cómo te fue belongs on the imperative.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009), on anteposed negative-polarity quantifiers

field: transformsOf, tense transform, rendered answer for bank:u53-0542
quote: Ayer Cada uní con su cuento: ese es el barrio.
problem: The clause parser reads the pronoun uno as first person of unir and conjugates it to uní. Other wrong outputs from the same survey of all 13,410 C1 rows: Antes Gracias, tenía razón. (u53-1645); Ayer de ser así, fuimos a juicio. (u53-0882); Antes Cada quien sabía lo suyo y calla lo ajeno. (u53-0543, half the sentence shifted). 349 of 2,126 Antes or Ayer answers leave a capital on the second word.
authority: morphology: uno is a pronoun here

quote: You only need to recognise it, never to say it.
problem: The script promises recognition only, and the owner's standing decision is no voseo, but nothing in the compiler treats this node as receptive. In 8 rendered days at u59 the learner gets 20 "How do you say this in Spanish?" cards ending in (vos) and must type answers such as Vos sos el único que me entiende. All 126 rows have an empty accept list, so the tú form the script tells them to use is marked wrong.
authority: owner standing decision; rendered with tools/playtest/render.ts 59 8

quote: So: read it, understand it as "if or whoever, later", and never use it yourself.
problem: The learner is then required to type it. Rendered at u60: "Those who live in the area will receive a notice." with the answer Quienes vivieren en la zona recibirán un aviso. All 127 rows have an empty accept list, so the correct modern Spanish Quienes vivan en la zona... is rejected in favour of a form the script forbids.
authority: rendered with tools/playtest/render.ts 60 8; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive as archaic outside legal language

field: bank:u52-0611 (and all 135 u52 rows targeting g:se-form-recognition)
quote: Me preocupó el hecho de que no llamase en toda la semana.
problem: grammar.json says "-ra for production; -se recognised". The 129 u51 rows carry the -ra sentence in accept, the 135 u52 rows carry nothing. matchTranslation rejects Me preocupó el hecho de que no llamara en toda la semana. against this row, so the form the course taught for production fails. 23 of these rows are also dialogue or to-a-friend speech, where -se is rare in Colombia.
authority: tested with matchTranslation; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas on -ra and -se as equivalent
replacement: accept: ["Me preocupó el hecho de que no llamara en toda la semana."]. Generate the same -ra accept for all 135 rows.

quote: De haber llegado antes, habríamos visto a Hernando.
problem: The checker has no equivalence for forms that are fully interchangeable in standard Spanish. Tested and rejected: De haber llegado antes, hubiéramos visto a Hernando. against this answer; El hecho de que no llamase me preocupa. against -ra. Hubiera in the result clause is at least as common as habría in Latin American speech, so a learner who writes correct Bogotá Spanish is marked wrong.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry on haber and the -ra form in the apodosis; Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish
replacement: Add two global variants to expandAccepted: -ra and -se in any imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, and habría + participle with hubiera + participle in the main clause of a past unreal condition.

quote: What follows is never a new fact. It is the first fact, made clearer.
problem: The script's own examples break this. Es caro; o sea, no lo podemos pagar and Hernando viene todos los días; o sea, conoce el café mejor que nadie add a conclusion, not a restatement. O sea and es decir both work as conclusive markers. A learner who believes the rule cannot explain half the examples and will not recognise the most frequent spoken use.
authority: Diccionario de particulas discursivas del espanol, entry o sea; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: What follows is the first idea made clearer, or what it comes down to.

quote: Hernando comes every day; I mean, he knows the café better than anyone.
problem: This o sea is conclusive, so "I mean" misrenders it. The natural English is "so".
authority: semantic reasoning
replacement: Hernando comes every day, so he knows the café better than anyone.

quote: I arrived late, I mean, I missed the speech.
problem: Conclusive o sea. Missing the speech follows from arriving late, it does not restate it.
authority: semantic reasoning
replacement: I arrived late, so I missed the speech.

quote: Note the *que* in *o sea que*: no *que*, no conclusion.
problem: False, and contradicted by g:reformulation, taught the day before: Es caro; o sea, no lo podemos pagar is a conclusion with no que. Also Llegué tarde; o sea, me perdí el discurso (u53-1223).
authority: Diccionario de particulas discursivas del espanol, entry o sea
replacement: Note the *que*: *o sea que* runs straight into the sentence, with no comma. *O sea* on its own takes a comma: *o sea, Tomás se queda*.

quote: Almost. To draw a conclusion with a full sentence, *o sea* needs its *que*.
problem: O sea, Tomás se queda is correct. What is wrong in the pitfall sentence is the missing comma or que, not the lack of que as such.
authority: punctuation norm; usage evidence
replacement: Almost. Join it with *que*, or put a comma after *o sea*.

quote: Ask yourself: pointed at, or still open?
problem: The model fails the script's first example. El hecho de que no llamara is a fact you can point to, and the script says so ("The fact isn't in doubt"), yet it takes the subjunctive. A learner applying the closing test gets the indicative. The better model already exists in this band: g:consecutive-advanced says de ahí que takes the subjunctive "because you are not announcing the result as news". That one axis covers lo que digas, el hecho de que, aunque seas and de ahí que.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009), on the indicative as assertion and the subjunctive as non-assertion
replacement: Ask yourself: am I putting this forward as news? News takes the indicative. Everything else takes the subjunctive: what is still open, and what is already known and you are only reacting to.

quote: El hecho de que no llamó me preocupa.
problem: The perfect subjunctive, probably the most natural form here for a recent event, is rejected. Tested with matchTranslation. The indicative, which the script calls the unusual choice, is accepted.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on subjunctive tense after a present main verb
replacement: accept: ["El hecho de que no llamó me preocupa.", "El hecho de que no haya llamado me preocupa."]

quote: *Como no vengas, me enojo* means *if you don't come, I'll get angry*.
problem: This is the striking half of the lesson and the title names it, but como + subjunctive appears only in this rule line. It is in no example, Read and Pick or Your Turn, so the indicative and subjunctive como are never contrasted.
authority: measured: no como + subjunctive in examples, readAndPick or yourTurn
replacement: Add to examples, readAndPick and yourTurn: Como no vengas, me enojo. = If you don't come, I'll get angry. (to a friend)

quote: Teachers call these conditional clauses without *si*: *de* + compound infinitive, *como* + subjunctive, and the connectors *a no ser que* and *con tal de que*.
problem: Conditional como + subjunctive is much more typical of Spain than of Colombia, where si no vienes is the everyday form. The course gives it to Bogotá speakers with no regional note (ch202: Como no respire, mija, se me desmaya; Y como alguien me ponga corbata, me levanto). A learner will take it for the normal local threat.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009); confidence limited, no corpus access
replacement: Teachers call these conditional clauses without *si*: *de* + compound infinitive, *como* + subjunctive, and the connectors *a no ser que* and *con tal de que*. *Como* with the subjunctive is more common in Spain; in Colombia most people would say *si no llegas*.

quote: *Future for a guess:* *será caro, pero…* means "it may be expensive, but…". *Estará en el café* means "he's probably there".
problem: These are two different uses. Estará en el café is conjecture: the speaker does not know. Será caro, pero vale la pena is concession: the speaker usually does know and is granting the point. Calling both a guess teaches a learner to read será rico, pero no tiene modales as doubt about the money. The small print names both but the rule merges them.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on futuro de conjetura and futuro concesivo; Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish
replacement:
*Future for a guess:* *Estará en el café* means "he's probably there".

*Future to give way:* *será caro, pero…* grants the point before you answer it: "all right, it may be expensive, but…". You are not guessing.

quote: The future gives the guess "may be", then *pero* answers it.
problem: Same conflation.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: The future grants the point, "all right, it may be expensive", then *pero* answers it.

quote: The imperfect is for the past; for a plan, use the present.
problem: This sits in the lesson whose thesis is "Spanish tenses do not always mean their clock time", one day before p:imperfecto-citativo teaches Ernesto llegaba mañana, ¿no? (u53-0368). Mañana viajaba a Cali is grammatical: a plan that has fallen through, or one being checked.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on imperfecto prospectivo and citativo
replacement: For a fixed plan, use the present. *Viajaba* would sound as if the plan has fallen through.

quote: The imperfect softens the request; the preterite would say it already happened.
problem: Quise + infinitive normally means "tried to", often unsuccessfully: quise llamarte pero no pude. Nothing need have happened.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish on querer in the preterite
replacement: The imperfect softens the request; *quise* would report an attempt in the past, not a request now.

quote: It's going to be expensive, but it's worth it.
problem: Out of context this wrong option is a valid reading of Será muy caro, pero vale la pena, because a plain future is possible.
authority: semantic reasoning
replacement: It isn't expensive, but it's worth it.

quote: sit at the start of the sentence
problem: yourTurn[5].accept accepts Altamira ya compró tres edificios, por lo visto, and the bank uses mid and final position (u54-0433, u54-0737, u54-0756).
authority: internal contradiction
replacement: usually open the sentence, though they can also come in the middle or at the end,

quote: The verb takes the wish form, because you are pushing the idea away
problem: Nothing is wished here, so the label fights the explanation given in the same sentence. Band C1 uses "wish form" in 4 scripts and "subjunctive" in 4 others, sometimes in consecutive lessons of the same unit (u56 concessive says wish-form verb, u56 consecutive says subjunctive). Patterns add "maybe form" and "special form".
authority: measured across the 20 scripts
replacement: The verb takes the subjunctive, because you are pushing the idea away

quote: *¡Qué va!* on its own means "not at all". It is always a no.
problem: Qué va rejects what was just said, so after a negative question it opens a yes: ¿No te gustó? ¡Qué va, me encantó! A learner told it is always a no misreads that reply.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish; usage evidence
replacement: *¡Qué va!* rejects what was just said. After *¿Estás cansado?* it means "not at all". After *¿No te gustó?* it can open a yes: *¡Qué va, me encantó!*

quote: Almost. *Qué va* always means "not at all", so it can't go before a yes.
problem: Same point. The pitfall sentence is still wrong, but for a different reason.
authority: usage evidence
replacement: Almost. *Qué va* rejects what was just said, and here you are saying yes to it.

quote: For something you want now, use the plain wish form: *¡Si al menos llamara!*
problem: Across the course "wish form" means the present subjunctive (llame); g:imperfect-subj says you "switch" away from the wish forms to the -ra set. Calling llamara the plain wish form invites ¡Si al menos llame!
authority: measured: g_imperfect-subj.json rule
replacement: For something you want now, use the *-ra* form: *¡Si al menos llamara!*

quote: The wish is about now, so you need the plain wish form: *llamara*.
problem: Same point.
authority: measured
replacement: The wish is about now, so you need the *-ra* form: *llamara*.

quote: Pick *cuya* or *cuyas* and type the whole sentence: *Es una tienda ___ empleadas son todas mujeres.*
problem: The prompt ends todas mujeres and the answer ends todas de Cali. A learner who types the whole sentence as shown is marked wrong (tested). The prompt sentence is also a tautology.
authority: matchTranslation and checkExact both reject the prompt sentence
replacement: Pick *cuya* or *cuyas* and type the whole sentence: *Es una tienda ___ empleadas son todas de Cali.*

quote: the man whose daughters live in Cali
problem: The Spanish is a full sentence and the English drops the main clause, against the rule that the English is the exact translation. The two wrong options need the same change.
authority: owner standing decision
replacement: I know the man whose daughters live in Cali.

quote: a company whose owner lives in Miami
problem: The Spanish is a full sentence and the English drops the main clause, against the rule that the English is the exact translation. The two wrong options need the same change.
authority: owner standing decision
replacement: It's a company whose owner lives in Miami.

quote: a neighbourhood whose buildings are very old
problem: The Spanish is a full sentence and the English drops the main clause, against the rule that the English is the exact translation. The two wrong options need the same change.
authority: owner standing decision
replacement: It's a neighbourhood whose buildings are very old.

quote: an office whose rules are clear
problem: The Spanish is a full sentence and the English drops the main clause, against the rule that the English is the exact translation. The two wrong options need the same change.
authority: owner standing decision
replacement: It's an office whose rules are clear.

quote: No *el*, *la* or *su* follows it: *cuyos dueños*, never *cuyos los dueños*.
problem: At least 18 C1 bank rows use preposition + cuyo (u55-0027 a cuyo cargo, u55-0037 de cuyas preguntas), which is the commonest formal pattern, and the rule never mentions it.
authority: measured over 13,410 rows; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement:
No *el*, *la* or *su* follows it: *cuyos dueños*, never *cuyos los dueños*.
A preposition goes in front of it: *un proyecto de cuyo éxito depende todo el barrio*.

quote: *Por mucho que* and *por muy… que* take the subjunctive: the speaker grants any degree and the result stays the same.
problem: Por mucho que and por más que take the indicative for something that really happened: Por más que lo intentó, no pudo. No script and no row of the 72,693 shows this, so a learner will force the subjunctive on factual past effort and misread the indicative in every novel. u52-0266 Por mucho que lo negase, acabó por admitirlo and u44-0092 Por más que Tomás se esforzara, la palabra no le salía both narrate real events, where the indicative is the normal choice.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on concessive por mucho que with indicative; Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish
replacement: *Por mucho que* and *por muy… que* normally take the subjunctive: the speaker grants any degree and the result stays the same. For something that really happened, the indicative is normal: *Por más que lo intentó, no pudo*.

quote: Remember: *mucho* goes with a verb, *muy* with an adjective.
problem: Por mucho + noun is left out, and there mucho agrees: por mucha plata que tenga. Tarde in Read and Pick item 6 is an adverb, not an adjective.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: Remember: *mucho* goes with a verb, *muy* with an adjective or adverb. Before a noun, *mucho* agrees with it: *por mucha plata que tenga*.

quote: that sound like a writer, not like a teenager saying *aunque*
problem: Aunque is the neutral concessive of every register, including academic prose. Telling a C1 learner it sounds adolescent will push them into overusing si bien.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: that give a writer more range than *aunque* alone

quote: If the main sentence is in the past, the verb after *de ahí que* is the past subjunctive (*se aplazara*, *oyera*). If it is in the present, it is the present subjunctive (*pueda*).
problem: False. The tense follows the time of the consequence, not the first clause. The bank itself contradicts it: u56-0203 La ciudad creció sin plan; de ahí que el tráfico sea una pesadilla, and u57-0403 uses the perfect subjunctive hayan sorprendido.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on de ahí que; internal contradiction with bank rows
replacement: The tense follows the result, not the first sentence. A result in the past takes the past subjunctive (*se aplazara*, *oyera*). A result that holds now takes the present subjunctive (*pueda*), even after a past cause: *la ciudad creció sin plan; de ahí que el tráfico sea una pesadilla*.

quote: The main verb is in the present, so *de ahí que* needs the present subjunctive *pueda*.
problem: Same false tense rule.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: The result holds now, so *de ahí que* needs the present subjunctive *pueda*.

quote: Past main verb, so the past subjunctive *protestara* follows *de ahí que*.
problem: Same false tense rule.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: The result is in the past, so the past subjunctive *protestara* follows *de ahí que*.

quote: *De manera que* also takes a normal verb when you simply report what happened: *llegó tarde, de manera que perdió el vuelo*.
problem: The hook says the connector decides the mood, and "when you simply report" implies another case, but the other case is never stated. De manera que + subjunctive means purpose: habla despacio, de manera que te entiendan. Measured: no script and no bank row in the whole course contains it. This is the classic mood alternation of this connector.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish; measured over all scripts and 72,693 rows
replacement: *De manera que* also takes a normal verb when you simply report what happened: *llegó tarde, de manera que perdió el vuelo*. With the subjunctive it names a goal, not a result: *habla despacio, de manera que te entiendan* means "so that they understand you".

quote: The result usually uses *habría*.
problem: Hubiera is equally standard in the result clause and very common in Latin America, and the story itself uses an imperfect (ch202: De haber tenido más tiempo, traíamos a los de Medellín).
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry on haber; usage evidence
replacement: The result uses *habría* or *hubiera*.

quote: De haber llegado antes habríamos visto a Hernando.
problem: De haber llegado antes, hubiéramos visto a Hernando is rejected (tested). A global checker variant is the better fix; this is the content-level stopgap.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas
replacement: accept: ["De haber llegado antes habríamos visto a Hernando.", "De haber llegado antes, hubiéramos visto a Hernando."]

quote: *De* + *haber* + *-ado/-ido* looks back: *de haberlo sabido*, "had I known".
problem: De + simple infinitive, the commoner form, is left out: de ser así, de seguir así, de no ser por. The course knows de ser así as a chunk (u53-1926) but never connects it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on condicionales de infinitivo
replacement: *De* + *haber* + *-ado/-ido* looks back: *de haberlo sabido*, "had I known". *De* + the plain verb looks at now or next: *de ser así*, "if so".

quote: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, siempre y cuando
problem: The script never contains siempre y cuando. It says "four ways" and teaches de haber, como, a no ser que and con tal de que.
authority: measured
replacement: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, con tal de que

quote: The verbs stay normal: *Cuanto más practico, mejor hablo.*
problem: Two omissions make this false. For the future the first verb takes the subjunctive, and the bank does this while the rule says otherwise (u58-0133 Cuanto menos peso lleves, más lejos llegarás; u58-0186 Cuanto menos ruido hagas, mejor). Before a noun, cuanto agrees: cuanta más gente, cuantos más días. Silence on agreement is why six rows are wrong (see the following claims).
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on proportional correlatives; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry cuanto
replacement: For habits and facts the verbs stay normal: *Cuanto más practico, mejor hablo.* For something still to come, the first verb takes the subjunctive: *Cuanto más practiques, mejor hablarás.* Before a noun, *cuanto* agrees with it: *cuanta más plata tengo, más gasto*.

quote: Cuanto menos plata hay, más se cuida cada peso.
problem: Cuanto agrees with the noun it quantifies, and this noun is feminine. The bank has no row at all with cuanta or cuantos, so the learner only ever sees the unagreed form and will reproduce it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on proportional correlatives; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry cuanto
replacement: Cuanta menos plata hay, más se cuida cada peso.

quote: Cuanto menos nieve cae, más pequeño se ve el glaciar.
problem: Cuanto agrees with the noun it quantifies, and this noun is feminine. The bank has no row at all with cuanta or cuantos, so the learner only ever sees the unagreed form and will reproduce it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on proportional correlatives; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry cuanto
replacement: Cuanta menos nieve cae, más pequeño se ve el glaciar.

quote: Cuanto menos nieve cae, más pequeño es el glaciar.
problem: Cuanto agrees with the noun it quantifies, and this noun is feminine. The bank has no row at all with cuanta or cuantos, so the learner only ever sees the unagreed form and will reproduce it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on proportional correlatives; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry cuanto
replacement: Cuanta menos nieve cae, más pequeño es el glaciar.

quote: Cuanto más lluvia cae, más barro hay en el camino.
problem: Cuanto agrees with the noun it quantifies, and this noun is feminine. The bank has no row at all with cuanta or cuantos, so the learner only ever sees the unagreed form and will reproduce it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on proportional correlatives; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry cuanto
replacement: Cuanta más lluvia cae, más barro hay en el camino.

quote: Cuanto menos luz entra, más frío se siente el cuarto.
problem: Cuanto agrees with the noun it quantifies, and this noun is feminine. The bank has no row at all with cuanta or cuantos, so the learner only ever sees the unagreed form and will reproduce it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on proportional correlatives; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry cuanto
replacement: Cuanta menos luz entra, más frío se siente el cuarto.

quote: Cuanto más prisa tengo, peor escribo.
problem: Cuanto agrees with the noun it quantifies, and this noun is feminine. The bank has no row at all with cuanta or cuantos, so the learner only ever sees the unagreed form and will reproduce it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on proportional correlatives; RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry cuanto
replacement: Cuanta más prisa tengo, peor escribo.

problem: Accept list is empty. g:comparatives-advanced taught Mientras más trabajo, menos duermo as the main form and accepts Entre más, but here Mientras más practico, mejor hablo. is rejected (tested). The learner is marked wrong for what the course taught, and for what people say in Bogotá.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry mientras; tested with matchTranslation
replacement: accept: ["Mientras más practico, mejor hablo.", "Entre más practico, mejor hablo."]

problem: Same rejection for Mientras más lo pienso, menos lo entiendo.
authority: tested with matchTranslation
replacement: accept: ["Mientras más lo pienso, menos lo entiendo.", "Entre más lo pienso, menos lo entiendo."]

quote: The more I think, the less I understand.
problem: The Spanish has lo twice; examples[0] renders it "about it" and "it". The option is not the exact translation.
authority: owner standing decision
replacement: The more I think about it, the less I understand it.

quote: *Apenas* + past: "barely had we... when". It is quick and sudden.
problem: In Colombia apenas is the everyday "as soon as", and it works for the future too. The rule restricts it to the past, while the bank already uses it with the subjunctive from u32 on (u37-0080 Quiero que me llames apenas llegues; u45-0798 Yo te pongo al tanto apenas llegue Mariana; u50-1567). The C1 rule is narrower than what the learner has been reading for 20 units, and the unit then gives 58 rows to nada más + infinitive instead.
authority: usage evidence; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: *Apenas*: "as soon as", the everyday choice in Colombia. About the past, use a past verb: *Apenas abrimos, llegó Hernando* ("we had barely opened when..."). About the future, use the same form as *en cuanto*: *Apenas llegue, te aviso*.

quote: Teachers call these temporal conjunctions.
problem: Nada más + infinitive leads this lesson with 58 C1 rows and no regional note, yet it is chiefly a Spain construction and is not how a Bogotá speaker would say it (Nada más terminar la viga, llámame; ¿Vas a llamar nada más llegar?). It is fine for recognition and writing, but the course presents it as the default.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009); confidence limited, no corpus access
replacement: Teachers call these temporal conjunctions. *Nada más* + infinitive is mostly Spanish from Spain and formal writing; in Bogotá people say *apenas* or *en cuanto*.

quote: *La mitad* (half) behaves like *la mayoría*: *la mitad se fue* or *se fueron*.
problem: The title promises el resto and the script never covers its agreement. The commonest English-speaker surprise in this area is missing too: when you belong to the group, the verb can be first person plural.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry concordancia; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: *La mitad* (half) behaves like *la mayoría*: *la mitad se fue* or *se fueron*. *El resto de* works the same way. If you belong to the group, the verb can say so: *la mayoría de los vecinos votamos en contra*.

quote: You know *ser* for what something is and *estar* for how or where. Four small frames sharpen them:
problem: The title says "at the edges" but the four frames are mostly B1 phrases, and La mesa es de madera is A2. Nothing here deals with actual C1 ser and estar: resultative estar versus passive ser (la tienda está cerrada, fue cerrada), estar + adjective for a perceived change (estás muy joven), estar que + verb, es para tanto, estar en (el problema está en que...), ser de + infinitive (es de esperar).
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish

quote: The *tú* commands are *ven* and *siéntate*: the *d* disappears from *vení*.
problem: Vení has no d. The sentence appears to have been built from Spain's venid.
authority: orthography
replacement: The *tú* commands are *ven* and *siéntate*: *vení* loses its last vowel and *sentate* gets its *ie* back.

quote: Vale does it all the time when she is happy or angry.
problem: False. Across all 219 chapters the only voseo word is the wrong option Que aprenda a hablar de vos in a ch213 question, and the 270 scenes have none. Vale speaks tú throughout (ch184: Conmigo dices las cosas que son tuyas).
authority: measured with a search over app/content/story and app/content/scenes

quote: You will hear it all through Vale's story.
problem: Same false promise. Either add paisa voseo to the Medellín chapters at the end of the course, which is the stronger option, or remove the claim.
authority: measured

quote: Commands also put the stress at the end: *vení* (*ven*), *sentate* (*siéntate*).
problem: Rows use forms this rule never prepares: Vos sabés que acá siempre hay un plato para vos, Vos te enredás cuando hablás rápido, Sí, tomá. The learner needs to know vos follows prepositions and the object pronoun stays te.
authority: measured against bank rows; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: Commands also put the stress at the end: *vení* (*ven*), *sentate* (*siéntate*). After a preposition it stays *vos* (*para vos*, *con vos*), and the object word stays *te*: *¿vos te acordás?*

quote: Quien bien amare, tarde olvidará.
problem: The saying is Quien bien ama, tarde olvida. The -re version is invented and presented as a proverb, and u59-1206 attributes it to Hernando's grandfather.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Quien quisiere celeste, que le cueste, decía mi tío.
problem: The saying is Quien quiera celeste, que le cueste. The archaic form is invented.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Si algún día tuviere una hija, le pondré Rosa.
problem: A personal promise in the future subjunctive. pitfalls[2] says of this very use: "No one talks this way."
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Cuando el café estuviere listo, avisaré a todos.
problem: Everyday context, same contradiction with pitfalls[2].
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Si te vieres en problemas, escríbeme.
problem: Informal tú to a friend, same contradiction with pitfalls[2].
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Normal order puts the subject first: *El barrio ha cambiado mucho.*
problem: With verbs of arriving, appearing and remaining, the subject normally follows: se fue la luz, llegó Vale, queda poco. The lesson's own examples (Poco queda del edificio) have no subject to move. This is the last word-order lesson in the course and the only one a C1 learner gets; subject after the verb when the subject is the news is taught nowhere.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on subject position and informational focus; Bosque and Demonte, Gramatica descriptiva
replacement: With most verbs the subject comes first: *El barrio ha cambiado mucho.* With verbs like *llegar*, *quedar* and *faltar* it usually follows, because it is the news: *llegó Vale*.

quote: Type in Spanish: It's hard to say.
problem: The English gives no sign that fronting is wanted, the accept list is empty, and the correct neutral Spanish Es difícil decirlo. is rejected (tested). The learner is marked wrong for the more natural sentence.
authority: tested with matchTranslation and checkExact
replacement: Put the key word first: It's hard to say.

authority: tested with matchTranslation and checkExact

problem: The English gives no sign that fronting is wanted, the accept list is empty, and the correct neutral Spanish Queda poco del edificio original. is rejected (tested). The learner is marked wrong for the more natural sentence.
authority: tested with matchTranslation and checkExact

problem: The English gives no sign that fronting is wanted, the accept list is empty, and the correct neutral Spanish He aprendido mucho aquí. is rejected (tested). The learner is marked wrong for the more natural sentence.
authority: tested with matchTranslation and checkExact

quote: ¿Mucho has cambiado tú en estos años?
problem: Literary focus fronting turned into a yes or no question to a friend. Nobody asks this; the rule itself says the device belongs to "writing, speeches and reviews". These rows look like generated question variants, and they are served in production. Delete the row.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on focus fronting; usage evidence

problem: An absolute participle clause tacked onto a spoken question. The script says it "almost always comes first" and belongs to writing. Delete the row.

quote: It is a shortcut for "once that was done".
problem: No limit is given, so a learner will build Caminado el parque or Trabajada la mañana. The construction needs a verb with an end point: transitive or unaccusative, perfective in meaning.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on construcciones absolutas de participio
replacement: It is a shortcut for "once that was done", so it needs a verb with a finish line: *firmar*, *aprobar*, *terminar*, *llegar*. Open-ended verbs like *caminar* or *trabajar* do not work here.

quote: Who or what the action belongs to follows with *de*: *la llegada de Yesid*, *la venta del edificio*.
problem: The first example has a doer and the second has a thing done, and the rule treats them as one. When both are named, Spanish needs a second marker. Por parte de, the formal device this register depends on, is in no script, and it occurs in only 2 bank rows, neither with a noun of action.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on nominalisation and argument structure
replacement: Who or what the action belongs to follows with *de*: *la llegada de Yesid*, *la venta del edificio*. When you name both, the doer takes *por parte de*: *la compra del edificio por parte de Altamira*.

quote: In Latin America, *agarrar* is very common here. Never *coger*.
problem: Coger is vulgar in Mexico, Central America and the River Plate, but it is ordinary in Colombia, the story's setting: coger un taxi, coja la Séptima. "Never" is false there, and the bank never shows it (0 rows), so a learner is warned off a word they will hear daily in Bogotá and may think it obscene. Avoiding it for neutral production is defensible; the blanket claim is not.
authority: Diccionario de americanismos (ASALE); usage evidence
replacement: In Latin America, *agarrar* is very common here. Avoid *coger* in Mexico or Argentina, where it is vulgar. In Colombia it is ordinary and you will hear it all the time.

quote: In Latin America you *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is the Spain word, and best avoided here.
problem: Same point. Cojo el bus en la 72 is normal Bogotá Spanish, and it is listed as wrong.
authority: Diccionario de americanismos (ASALE); usage evidence
replacement: Across Latin America you can always *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is fine in Colombia but vulgar in Mexico and Argentina, so *tomar* is the safe choice.

quote: Almost. In Latin America *coger* is best avoided, so say *agarró* (or *tomó*).
problem: Same point, more mildly put.
authority: Diccionario de americanismos (ASALE); usage evidence
replacement: Almost. *Coger* is vulgar in some countries, so *agarró* (or *tomó*) is the safe choice.

quote: Watch out: *ignorar* is not *to ignore someone*.
problem: False as stated. "Not to pay attention to" is an established meaning in the DLE and the everyday one: me ignoró. The course's own bank uses it (u43-1103 Ignoré el aviso y salí sin abrigo; u43-1104 no quiero ignorar tus ideas). A learner who believes this misreads ordinary Spanish and sees a contradiction with u43.
authority: RAE, Diccionario de la lengua espanola, entry ignorar, sense 2
replacement: Watch out: *ignorar* can mean "to take no notice of" (*me ignoró*), but in a formal text like these it means you lack the information.

quote: with *ignorar* as a false friend
problem: A partial false friend at most.
authority: RAE, Diccionario de la lengua espanola
replacement: with *ignorar* as a partial false friend

quote: to not know
problem: The gloss covers one sense while bank rows in u43 use the other, so hover glosses and meaning cards contradict the sentence.
authority: RAE, Diccionario de la lengua espanola
replacement: to not know; to ignore

quote: Two moods, as in *si* sentences you already know:
problem: Both cases named are subjunctive, one present and one imperfect. They are two tenses of one mood. A learner studying mood choice is told the opposite of what the examples show.
authority: grammatical terminology
replacement: Two tenses of the subjunctive, as in *si* sentences you already know:

quote:
¿Estás por llamar a la editorial?
Estoy por todo, pero me da miedo.
problem: Estar por needs an infinitive here. Estoy por todo is not idiomatic Spanish and does not mean "I'm thinking of everything". The English needs matching: "I'm about to, but I'm scared" and "I'm about to decide". The sentences look like a mechanical echo of the frame.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009); usage evidence
replacement:
¿Estás por llamar a la editorial?
Estoy por hacerlo, pero me da miedo.

quote:
¿Estás por vender?
Estoy por todo, y por nada.
problem: Estar por needs an infinitive here. Estoy por todo is not idiomatic Spanish and does not mean "I'm thinking of everything". The English needs matching: "I'm about to, but I'm scared" and "I'm about to decide". The sentences look like a mechanical echo of the frame.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009); usage evidence
replacement:
¿Estás por vender?
Estoy por decidirlo.

quote: ¿Quién asumió, sin leerlo, que todo estaba firmado?
problem: Asumir for "suppose" is an English calque, widespread but still avoided in careful Spanish, and this is the unit teaching dar por sentado.
authority: Fundeu on asumir; RAE, Diccionario de la lengua espanola
replacement: ¿Quién dio por sentado, sin leerlo, que todo estaba firmado?

quote: Arreglaron mi celular en una hora.
problem: Spanish marks the affected person with a pronoun rather than a possessive. Translated English at C1.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish on the dative of interest
replacement: Me arreglaron el celular en una hora.

quote: Yo tengo sesenta y ocho años y un taller cuyo techo se moja cada vez que llueve.
problem: A 68-year-old cobbler speaking aloud. g:cuyo-relatives says this form belongs to writing and formal speech and that "in chat people use two sentences". The grammar target overrides the character.
authority: register; the script's own rule
replacement: Yo tengo sesenta y ocho años y un taller al que se le moja el techo cada vez que llueve.
